ijaw_tamuno.name: create all things, partly identified with the sky
ijaw_tamuno.notes: Among the Kalabari and eastern Delta Ijaw the supreme being Tamuno (fem. Tamarau, 'Mother-Maker') is held to have made man, animals and trees, and is partly identified with the sky; lesser deities act as intermediaries to this high god.

sources.reference: Grokipedia, 'Kalabari tribe' (Tamuno the supreme creator); Mythlok, 'Ijaw mythology'

ijaw_tamuno.name: give each person a spiritual double (teme) and appoint the destiny chosen before birth
ijaw_tamuno.notes: As the creator power Tamuno/Woyengi grants each human a teme (soul/spiritual double) and ratifies the fate the unborn chooses before entering the world.

sources.reference: Mythlok, 'Ijaw mythology' (teme and the choice of destiny); Britannica, 'Woyengi'

inca_huallallo_carhuincho.name: blaze up in fiery flames that reach the sky
inca_huallallo_carhuincho.notes: When besieged by Pariacaca the fire-huaca turned his body to flames towering to the heavens; Pariacaca quenched him with cataracts of rain and landslides.

sources.reference: Huarochirí Manuscript (ch. 8-9, the contest of Pariacaca and Huallallo Carhuincho)

inca_huallallo_carhuincho.name: demand and devour human children of his subject Yunca
inca_huallallo_carhuincho.notes: Lord of the Yunca before Pariacaca, he allowed each family only two children and ate one of them.

inca_huallallo_carhuincho.name: summon a giant two-headed serpent (amaru)
inca_huallallo_carhuincho.notes: In his last defence he raised a huge two-headed snake; Pariacaca struck it with his golden staff and froze it into the stone amaru.

sources.reference: Huarochirí Manuscript (ch. 9, the amaru turned to stone)

inca_mama_killa.name: govern the lunar calendar, months and the timing of festivals
inca_mama_killa.notes: The Quechua word for month, quilla, is the word for moon; her phases set the Inca ritual and agricultural year and the reckoning of festivals.

inca_mama_killa.name: guard women, marriage and fertility
inca_mama_killa.notes: As consort of Inti she was patroness of women and marriage and protectress of female fertility, her cycle linked to menstruation.

sources.reference: Ancient Pages, 'Mama Quilla, Incan Moon Goddess of Marriage and Fertility'

inca_pariacaca.name: defeat, quench and banish the fire-god Huallallo Carhuincho
inca_pariacaca.notes: The structural core of the Huarochirí cycle: the storm-and-water god overwhelms the fire-and-drought huaca with rain and flood and drives him to the Anti lowlands.

inca_pariacaca.name: take the form of a falcon (hatun-falcon)
inca_pariacaca.notes: Born of the five falcon-eggs of Condorcoto, he and his fivefold self can assume falcon shape.

sources.reference: Huarochirí Manuscript (ch. 5, the five eggs and falcons)

inti.name: send forth Manco Cápac and the first Inca to found Cuzco
inti.notes: As divine father of the dynasty Inti dispatches the founders with the golden staff to seek the site of his temple.

sources.reference: Britannica, 'Inti'; Garcilaso de la Vega, Comentarios Reales (Lake Titicaca origin)

inkarri.name: regenerate his buried body upward from the severed head
inkarri.notes: The decapitated Inca king's head, buried in Cuzco, slowly grows a new body from the head down; when complete he will return and reverse the conquered order in a pachakuti.

sources.reference: Wikipedia, 'Inkarri'; documented from Q'ero informants (Arguedas, mid-20th c.)

insikiran.name: descend as a benevolent son of the sun (Wei)
insikiran.notes: In the Pemon/Macuxi cycle Insikiran (Inshkirung) is the benevolent brother, a child of Wei the sun and bearer of its life-principle, set against his malevolent brother Makunaima.

sources.reference: Grokipedia, 'Macuxi' (Insikiran and Makunaima, sons of Wei); Koch-Grünberg, Vom Roroima zum Orinoco

inca_manco_capac.name: teach men agriculture, law and the civilized arts
inca_manco_capac.notes: In the Garcilaso tradition the first Sapa Inca, sent by Inti, instructed men in farming, building and government while Mama Ocllo taught the women.

sources.reference: Garcilaso de la Vega, Comentarios Reales de los Incas (bk. 1)

inuit_sedna.name: give rise to the sea-mammals from her severed finger-joints
inuit_sedna.notes: Cast from her father's boat, she clung to the gunwale until he cut off her fingers joint by joint; the falling joints became the seals, then the walrus, then the whales, and she sank to rule them on the sea floor.

sources.reference: Wikipedia, 'Sedna (mythology)'; Rasmussen, Intellectual Culture of the Iglulik Eskimos

inuit_anningan.name: drive a dog-sledge abroad to hunt seals when the moon wanes
inuit_anningan.notes: In the waning quarter the hungry Moon Man harnesses his dogs and leaves to hunt seals, disappearing some days (the new moon) before returning full; his neglect of food in pursuit of his sister explains the thinning crescent.

sources.reference: Wikipedia, 'Sun and Moon (Inuit myth)'; Windows to the Universe, 'Anningan'

ijaw_ogboinba.name: strip and absorb the magical powers of those she defeats
ijaw_ogboinba.notes: Journeying back to confront the creatress, the sorceress overcame and took the powers of a succession of guardian-figures, growing ever stronger until she challenged Woyengi herself.

ijaw_ogboinba.name: take refuge inside the pupil of a pregnant woman's eye
ijaw_ogboinba.notes: Defeated and stripped of her powers by Woyengi, she fled into the eyes of a pregnant woman; the Ijaw say it is Ogboinba who looks back from every human eye.

ijaw_woyengi.name: great chair and table of creation

sources.reference: Mythlok, 'Woyengi' (seated on a great chair at a table heaped with earth)

inti.name: golden face-disc radiating rays and flames

inca_illapa.name: celestial water-jar of the Milky Way (struck to release rain)

sources.reference: Ancient Pages, 'Illapa'; Encyclopedia.com, 'Illapa' (the jar of the celestial river)

inca_viracocha.name: thunderbolts held in either hand (Gateway of the Sun staff-god)

sources.reference: World History Encyclopedia, 'Viracocha' (Gate of the Sun, Tiwanaku)

inca_pariacaca.name: golden staff (used to petrify the amaru)

inca_manco_capac.name: royal fringe (mascapaicha) and llautu headband of the Sapa Inca

inkarri.name: the buried severed head of the Inca king (from which the body regrows)

inca_supay.name: offerings of coca, alcohol and tobacco in the mine (later El Tío)

sources.reference: Grokipedia, 'Supay'; godsandmonsters.info, 'Andes Mythology' (El Tío of the mines)

inca_mama_ocllo.name: backstrap loom and spindle (the weaving she taught the women)

sources.reference: Garcilaso de la Vega, Comentarios Reales de los Incas (Mama Ocllo teaches spinning and weaving)

inuit_sedna.name: her tangled hair, combed and braided by the shaman in propitiation

sources.reference: Wikipedia, 'Sedna (mythology)' (the shaman combs her filth-laden hair)

ijaw_tamuno.gloss: the Mother-Maker; feminine form of the creator

ijaw_woyengi.name: Invocation of the Great Mother for fertility and destiny
ijaw_woyengi.cadence: as petition, especially for children and at birth
ijaw_woyengi.notes: The supreme creatress is appealed to for children and for the destiny chosen before birth; petitioners (as in the Ogboinba narrative) journey to her presence to ask a child, healing or magical power, the canonical Ijaw dramatization of the irreversibility of her destiny-decree.

sources.reference: Britannica, 'Woyengi'; Oriire, 'Woyengi and Ogboinba: The Ijaw Creation Story'

inti.name: Inti Raymi, the Festival of the Sun
inti.notes: The greatest Inca state festival, held at the winter solstice when the sun's power seemed most fragile; the Sapa Inca raised a cup of chicha to Inti and poured it on the ground, with sacrifices of llamas, cloth and chicha and a priestly pilgrimage to the east. At the Coricancha the aclla ('chosen women') wove cloth and brewed chicha for the Sun.

inti.name: Cult of the Sun at the Coricancha
inti.notes: The gold-plated Temple of the Sun at Cuzco, the most sacred huaca of the empire and the centre of the Inca world, housed the golden image of Inti and the mummies of dead rulers; at dawn the sun struck a great golden disc within the eastern chamber. The state cult of Inti was imposed throughout Tahuantinsuyu.

inca_mama_killa.name: Coya Raymi, the Queen's Festival
inca_mama_killa.cadence: annual, in September (the spring equinox / onset of the rains)
inca_mama_killa.notes: The September festival of the moon-goddess, honouring women and fertility and inaugurating the rainy season; it included the Situa purification driving sickness from Cuzco. Her silver-clad shrine within the Coricancha was served by priestesses.

sources.reference: Ancient Pages, 'Mama Quilla'; Guaman Poma, Nueva Corónica (Coya Raymi Quilla)

inca_pachamama.name: Pago a la tierra / despacho (payment to the earth)
inca_pachamama.cadence: at planting and especially in August, the month the earth 'opens'
inca_pachamama.notes: Buried offerings to the earth-mother of coca leaves, chicha, llama fat (and formerly guinea pig, shells, and gold/silver figurines), prepared by an Andean ritual specialist (paqo) in reciprocity for the soil's fertility; the August earth-feasts remain the living core of her cult.

inca_pariacaca.name: Mountain cult and pilgrimage to Pariacaca
inca_pariacaca.cadence: calendrical, with sacrifices at the snow-peak shrine
inca_pariacaca.notes: The fivefold storm-god was the chief huaca of the Huarochirí peoples descended from his five falcons; his snow-capped cordillera (over 5,700 m, sourcing the Rímac, Lurín, Mala and Cañete) was a pilgrimage shrine where the allied ayllus gathered to sacrifice and renew their bond to him.

sources.reference: Huarochirí Manuscript (the cult and pilgrimage of Pariacaca)

inca_supay.name: Underground offerings to the lord of the mine (El Tío)
inca_supay.notes: As lord of Uku Pacha and 'Lord of Metals' Supay is propitiated underground so that ore and miners return safely; the rite survives in Andean mines as offerings of coca, alcohol and tobacco to the horned figure El Tío.

inca_mama_sara.name: Veneration of the maize-mother doll (saramama / huantay sara)
inca_mama_sara.notes: The maize-mother was worshipped in a doll made of maize stalks, dressed and renewed at every harvest; unusual multi-eared or twin maize was kept as a manifestation of her spirit and reverenced to secure the crop's increase.

sources.reference: Wikipedia, 'Inca mythology' (saramama / huantay sara); Cobo, Historia del Nuevo Mundo

inuit_sedna.name: Comb-the-hair propitiation by the angakkuq
inuit_sedna.cadence: in time of famine, by the shaman's spirit-journey
inuit_sedna.notes: When game failed, the angakkuq made a trance spirit-descent to the sea floor to reach the mistress of the animals, whose tangled, filth-laden hair held the broken taboos of the people; combing and dressing her hair (her own fingerless hands cannot) appeased her so she released the seals, walrus and whales.

sources.reference: Wikipedia, 'Sedna (mythology)'; Rasmussen, Intellectual Culture of the Iglulik Eskimos (Takanakapsaluk)

inuit_nanook.name: Hosting the slain bear's soul with gendered tools
inuit_nanook.cadence: for several days after each polar-bear kill
inuit_nanook.notes: The killed bear's soul was honoured so its master would send bears again: the hide and skull were hung in the house for a set number of days and presented with tools of the bear's sex (a female bear with ulu, qulliq lamp, needles and thread; a male with knife and hunting gear), then the spirit released.

sources.reference: Wikipedia, 'Nanook'; documented among the Iglulik Inuit (Rasmussen, Fifth Thule Expedition)

inuit_pinga.name: Offerings to the keeper of the caribou
inuit_pinga.notes: Among the Iglulik Inuit, sacrificial offerings to Pinga, 'the one up there', secured success in the caribou hunt; she watches the conduct of the living and receives the souls of the dead before their possible rebirth.

sources.reference: Wikipedia, 'Pinga (goddess)'; Rasmussen, Intellectual Culture of the Iglulik Eskimos

attributes.name: descends from the sky in a bolt of lightning
attributes.notes: The Great Mother is said to have emerged from the sky in lightning to seat herself at the table of creation.

attributes.name: breathes life into the earth-moulded, genderless first humans
attributes.notes: She moulds humans from dirt, then embraces each and breathes life and chosen gender into them.

attributes.name: golden face-disc with radiating rays, or a seated golden boy (Punchao) with a royal headband
attributes.notes: Inti's chief image, the Punchao, was a small seated golden boy from whose head and shoulders rays shone, wearing the royal headband, with snakes and lions issuing from his body; its hollow belly held the ashes of dead rulers' organs. Gold was the 'sweat of the sun'.

attributes.name: frontal staff-god holding a staff (or thunderbolt) in each hand, crowned with rays ending in puma-heads, and weeping
attributes.notes: The Gateway of the Sun figure at Tiwanaku, the type associated with him: a radiate weeping deity gripping staffs/thunderbolts, flanked by running winged attendants; the tears are read as rain.

sources.reference: World History Encyclopedia, 'Viracocha' (Gate of the Sun)

attributes.name: wandering bearded old man in poor dress carrying a staff
attributes.notes: In the Andean creator-narratives he walks the land as a ragged elder teaching the peoples, then departs westward over the sea.

attributes.name: radiant warrior in shining garments whirling a sling, the lightning his sling-stone
attributes.notes: He stands in the Milky Way in bright dress; the crack of his sling is the thunderclap and its flash the lightning, while striking his sister's water-jar releases the rain.

attributes.name: silver disc bearing a human face; her shrine and image plated in silver
attributes.notes: The moon was seen as a great silver disc whose markings were her features; in the Coricancha her sanctuary and image were covered in silver, as Inti's were in gold. Lunar eclipses were read as an animal attacking her.

attributes.name: horned lord of the underworld (later the horned El Tío of the mines)
attributes.notes: An ambivalent ruler of Uku Pacha rather than a purely evil devil; survives as the horned, seated El Tío to whom miners make offerings underground.

attributes.name: doll fashioned of maize stalks, dressed and renewed each harvest
attributes.notes: Her venerated embodiment; multi-eared or deformed maize stalks were preserved as living manifestations of the goddess.

sacredPlants.name: willow tree (with which she is associated)

sacredAnimals.name: falcon (his fivefold birth-form from the five eggs of Condorcoto)

attributes.name: Sapa Inca in the royal fringe (mascapaicha) and multicoloured llautu headband
attributes.notes: Founder-king shown with the imperial red fringe hung from the llautu, the emblem of Inca sovereignty originating with the founding pair.

attributes.name: woman's head and torso with the tail of a marine mammal, her hands fingerless or maimed
attributes.notes: Sculpted as a mermaid-like figure; her lost fingers (cut off as she clung to the boat) mark why she cannot tend her own hair and must be combed by the shaman.

sacredAnimals.name: seal, walrus and whale (born of her finger-joints and held under her rule)

attributes.name: the great polar bear itself, a sentient master-animal accorded human-like respect
attributes.notes: Nanook is the archetype and lord of the polar bears (Inuktitut nanuq), treated as a soul-bearing person whose goodwill the bear-hunter must win.

attributes.name: the waxing-and-waning Moon, a hunter on a dog-drawn sledge, soot on his face
attributes.notes: The Moon Man's thinning and disappearance trace the lunar phases; the dark lunar markings are the soot his sister smeared on him to expose her night visitor.

attributes.name: the Sun, a fleeing woman bearing a torch, her brother's blackened by soot
attributes.notes: Both siblings seized torches as she fled; hers blazed bright and became the sun, his guttered to the dimmer moon. She had marked his face with soot/lampblack to reveal him.

sources.reference: Wikipedia, 'Sun and Moon (Inuit myth)'; Windows to the Universe, 'Malina'

attributes.name: formless indweller of the air; among Netsilik and Copper Inuit a giant naked infant (Naarjuk) whose breath is the wind
attributes.notes: Usually without fixed form, the life-force pervading the cosmos and weather; personified as the orphan giant-baby Naarjuk whose stirrings raise storms, which the shaman calms by tightening his garment.

sources.reference: Wikipedia, 'Silap Inua'; Saladin d'Anglure (Naarjuk among the Netsilik)

attributes.name: first Coya at the loom, teaching women to spin and weave
attributes.notes: The founding queen is figured with the distaff and backstrap loom as the bringer of the domestic and textile arts to Andean women.

sources.reference: Garcilaso de la Vega, Comentarios Reales de los Incas
